introduction-reimagining-the-relational-.core: Aurora keeps MySQL/PostgreSQL compatibility but separates compute from a distributed, log-structured storage layer. The database ships only redo log records to storage, which builds pages itself, cutting network I/O, speeding failover and letting replicas share the same storage.

first_principles.problem: Traditional RDS replication copies whole data pages and binlogs, making replicas lag and failover slow.
truths: Writing full pages repeatedly wastes I/O.
The log is the source of truth.
Shared storage avoids copying data to replicas.
derivation: **Failover** by promoting a replica in seconds.

analogy.title: Sending recipe edits instead of reprinting the cookbook
analogy.story: Kitchens receive only the change notes and update their own copies.
analogy.breaks: Kitchens interpret notes; Aurora storage applies logs deterministically.

example.title: Write path
flow: MySQL: data pages + doublewrite + binlog + redo
Aurora: redo log records to 6 storage copies

check.q: What does an Aurora writer send to storage?
check.a: Only redo log records; storage nodes build the data pages.

aurora-storage-architecture-6-copies-3-a.core: Aurora storage splits data into 10 GB protection groups, each with six copies across three AZs. Writes need 4 of 6 acknowledgements and reads 3 of 6 (quorum), so Aurora tolerates losing an entire AZ plus one more node for reads, and an AZ for writes. Storage auto-grows to 128 TiB and self-heals.

first_principles.problem: A single AZ outage or disk failure shouldn't lose data or block writes.

analogy.title: Six witnesses in three towns
analogy.story: A statement counts if four agree; you can lose a whole town and still reach agreement.
analogy.breaks: Witnesses can disagree on facts; storage copies converge deterministically from logs.

check.q: Why can Aurora keep writing after losing an AZ?
check.a: Losing one AZ removes 2 of 6 copies, leaving 4, which still meets the 4/6 write quorum.

endpoints-how-to-connect.core: Aurora provides a cluster (writer) endpoint that always points to the current primary, a reader endpoint that load-balances across replicas, instance endpoints for specific nodes, and custom endpoints for groups of instances. Applications split reads and writes by endpoint, and DNS updates on failover.

first_principles.problem: Apps hard-code the primary instance hostname and break after failover.
truths: Failover changes which instance is primary.
derivation: Keep **DNS TTL low** / use RDS Proxy or smart drivers.

analogy.title: A company's main phone number
analogy.story: Calls route to whoever is on duty, even when staff change.
analogy.breaks: Phone systems switch instantly; DNS caching can delay failover unless clients respect TTLs.

check.q: Which endpoint should an app use for writes?
check.a: The cluster (writer) endpoint, which always points to the current primary.

aurora-serverless-v2-instant-scaling.core: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity in fine-grained ACUs (Aurora Capacity Units, ~2 GiB memory each) within seconds, based on load, between a configured min and max, without dropping connections. It can mix with provisioned instances in one cluster and suits spiky, unpredictable or multi-tenant workloads.

first_principles.problem: A database sized for peak sits mostly idle, or a fixed size can't handle sudden spikes.
truths: Load varies by hour and day.
Capacity has a floor for warm caches.
derivation: Set **min** high enough for buffer cache.

analogy.title: An accordion
analogy.story: It expands and contracts smoothly as the music demands.
analogy.breaks: Accordions have no minimum; v2 needs a minimum ACU, and steady loads may be cheaper provisioned.

check.q: When might provisioned Aurora be cheaper than Serverless v2?
check.a: For steady, predictable high load, where reserved provisioned capacity costs less per hour.

aurora-global-database-speed-of-light-re.core: Aurora Global Database replicates storage from a primary region to up to five secondary regions with typically < 1 second lag, using dedicated storage-level replication rather than the database engine. Secondaries serve local reads and can be promoted for disaster recovery (RPO ~1 s, RTO ~minutes), or switched over planned.

first_principles.problem: A global app needs fast local reads worldwide and regional disaster recovery.
truths: Engine replication adds load and lag.
DR needs a warm copy elsewhere.
derivation: **Write forwarding** for occasional writes from secondaries.

analogy.title: A newspaper printed simultaneously in several cities
analogy.story: The master edition is edited in one city; presses elsewhere print it within a second.
analogy.breaks: Newspapers are read-only elsewhere; write forwarding lets secondaries send writes back to the primary.

check.q: Why does Global Database use storage-level replication?
check.a: It avoids engine overhead and achieves lower lag than logical/binlog replication.

aurora-vs-rds-choosing-the-right-tool.core: RDS runs standard engines (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, Db2) on EBS with Multi-AZ standby. Aurora offers higher performance, faster failover, up to 15 low-lag replicas, auto-growing storage, Serverless v2 and Global Database, at a higher price per hour and with I/O-based or I/O-optimized pricing. Choose by engine, scale, availability needs and cost.

first_principles.problem: A small internal app runs on Aurora and costs more than needed; a high-scale app on RDS struggles with replica lag.
truths: Aurora's architecture costs more but scales better.
Some engines exist only on RDS.
I/O pricing matters for heavy workloads.
derivation: **High scale, many replicas, fast failover** → Aurora.
**Small/steady** → RDS (or Aurora Serverless v2 for spiky).

analogy.title: A reliable saloon versus a performance car
analogy.story: Both get you there; one is cheaper to run, the other handles much more.
analogy.breaks: Cars can't change engines; you can migrate RDS to Aurora with a snapshot or replica.

example.title: Two decisions
flow: Internal CRUD app, 50 QPS → RDS PostgreSQL Multi-AZ
Consumer app, 20k QPS reads, global → Aurora + Global Database

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Pay for Aurora when you use its strengths.

check.q: Which engines require RDS rather than Aurora?
check.a: Oracle, SQL Server, Db2 and MariaDB.
